# Document Architecture

Durable documents exist to give one real reader a discoverable current authority. Use the simplest shape that preserves that authority, its links, and the reader's ability to act. TaskNotes follow [[claude/rules/tasks-rules]] instead of this document's body guidance.

## Authority and lifecycle

Apply the authority requirement in [[claude/CLAUDE-global#Operational Baseline]] through document lifecycle and provenance. Use `current` for a presently authoritative version, `evergreen` for a continuously maintained authority without a version chain, `draft` for non-authoritative work, and `archived` for history. When authority moves, the new owner states current truth and the predecessor becomes archived with `superseded_by`; a derived file names its true upstream with `source` and yields on conflict.

Project-scoped documents carry a vault-absolute project wikilink. New or substantively edited typed documents declare their actual author and concrete reader when a real consumer needs those fields; path-specific runtime contracts may define their own frontmatter. Do not invent a closed vault-wide type catalog that current consumers do not enforce.

## Placement and links

Place project documents under `pages/projects/<project>/`, rules/skills/charters in their canonical `claude/` homes, and templates under `templates/`. Vault prose uses resolvable vault-absolute wikilinks without `.md`; raw filesystem paths belong only in executable instructions. Move/rename through Obsidian when link resolution matters.

Reference the semantic owner instead of copying downstream fields, procedures, runtime versions, route tables, or status. A project `## Briefing` follows the L1 contract below; it is a derived ramp, never another owner of roadmap, task, or runtime facts. Backlinks make history discoverable but do not make every linked file current authority. Templates are starting scaffolds, not a second semantic SSOT.

## L1 Shared Alignment

L1 is the shared human-and-agent alignment layer for one project. It lets both readers answer why the project exists, which outcome is being validated now, what product or domain they are changing, how the project works, and where deeper authority lives. It does not absorb the authorities it routes to.

Every `type: project, stage: current` project page outside `templates/` declares one scalar `l1_entry`. The value is either one resolvable vault-absolute wikilink or one durable HTTPS repository URL. A vault-owned entry begins with these exact H2 sections in order:

1. `Briefing`
2. `Vision`
3. `Roadmap`
4. `Product / Domain Map`
5. `Workflow`
6. `Reading routes`

The roles may be concise and inline in the entry or split into linked semantic owners. A role is split only when its independent change cadence or reader value earns another document; no role gets an empty carrier. An external L1 entry uses the same roles in its owning repository. Its vault project page is a compatibility ramp that links the exact external entry and private project surfaces without reproducing a second Briefing, Vision, Roadmap, Product/Domain Map, or Workflow.

`Briefing` fits on one screen and contains only the current phase, the project-level outcome being validated, the current boundary, recent project-level changes that alter shared understanding, and routes for continuing. It projects from the role owners and live authority and yields to them on conflict. It contains no TaskNote inventory or status, owner list, commands, tests, deployment receipts, incident log, or file-by-file delivery history. Roadmap owns the current phase and evidence gates; periodic review reconciles Briefing against it and live reality.

The other roles divide semantic ownership as follows:

| Role | Owns |
| --- | --- |
| Vision | Commitments that, with the Human-Agent Principles, anchor derivation: mission, principles, long-term tradeoffs, and learning; plus concise foundational facts and hypotheses, distinguished from commitments, that serve as references testing derived conclusions |
| Roadmap | Current phase, project-level outcome, evidence gates, and next direction |
| Product / Domain Map | The user- or domain-level whole, boundaries among its parts, and routes to current behavior authorities |
| Workflow | How humans and agents collaborate, change shared truth, review evidence, and cross release or decision gates |
| Reading routes | Links to L1 roles and to deeper L2, product, runbook, TaskNote, runtime, or external authorities without copying them |

Important project decisions and their conditions live in a separate decision-history document linked from the Vision; the homepage keeps its current roles and the history entry point. Vision uses five sections: mission, principles, understanding of reality, long-term tradeoffs, and learning. Link the project's information-sources directory beside the relevant premise or learning commitment; its footer needs only the history link.

L1 roles do not own Agent L2 topology or trust contracts, implementation details, code or API contracts, operating procedures, runtime state, task queues, or task-period evidence. Those owners remain separate even when the L1 entry links them.

A project homepage may append a clearly labeled derived dashboard outside the six alignment roles, after `Reading routes`. It projects research, task, and runtime records with traceable source bindings; it does not create another editable state owner or put execution detail in Briefing or Vision. An external L1 homepage may present the same projection at its owning surface while the vault compatibility ramp links it. Dashboard content, meaningful-change updates, pause handling, access boundaries, and target-client verification follow [[claude/rules/project-rsi#Dashboard]]; this document owns the placement and authority boundary, not a dashboard implementation.

When L1 authority moves, establish the target and migrate current consumers before retiring duplicate current prose. Preserve unique private research and historical rationale as history. A still-needed old path becomes a body-free compatibility pointer to the new authority and its archive; an external site or document is labeled projection or archive and never presented as a parallel editable owner.

Machines may validate the single `l1_entry`, local entry section order, target/link resolution, role reachability, external-pointer presence, and inventory coverage. They do not infer whether Briefing fits one screen, whether each role is semantically sufficient, whether two facts compete for ownership, whether roadmap and Briefing agree, or whether a retired definition returned under another name. Those require a qualified reader with project context.

### Vision qualification

This is the single document-quality standard for every project's Vision, including an inline Vision or one owned by an external repository. It operationalizes [[claude/CLAUDE-global#Human-Agent Principles]] and [[claude/CLAUDE-global#Project Vision]]; it adds no project values or execution authority. Templates, project reviews, improvement loops, and document/verifier consumers use this standard. A qualifying Vision lets a first reader understand the project and lets an agent derive supported choices from it, testing them against current facts, without inventing missing values. It need not predetermine every future decision.

Apply every criterion to the selected Vision's actual scope and maturity; state a reason when a conditional concern does not apply. These are semantic dimensions, not required extra headings, fixed-length answers, scores, or an obligation to re-run all probes on every task. A clearly labeled, decision-relevant hypothesis can qualify before it is proven; presenting it as established fact cannot. Existing documents are evaluated at the current decision without bulk rewriting unrelated content.

| ID | Criterion | Evidence of qualification / material failure to catch |
| --- | --- | --- |
| V01 | Identity and mission | A first reader can explain what the project is, why it exists, and the change it seeks. Essential names and concepts are explained; a slogan, technology label, or feature inventory alone is insufficient. |
| V02 | Beneficiaries and value | The intended beneficiaries, relevant needs or opportunities, and offered value are understandable. Identify materially affected parties and current alternatives where they explain the choice; avoid claiming imagined demand as observed need. |
| V03 | Commitments and inheritance | Project-specific commitments guide real choices and inherit applicable global principles by reference. They do not duplicate a competing constitution or silently import another project's priorities. |
| V04 | Facts, hypotheses, and evidence | Distinguish chosen commitments, observed facts, and empirical hypotheses. Keep the premises needed to understand the direction in the main text, with traceable evidence and scope where needed; stale or missing evidence limits the corresponding claim. |
| V05 | Causal reasoning and alternatives | Explain why the chosen direction could create the intended value, including load-bearing assumptions and reasons for important choices. Account for credible alternatives where they could change the decision; a polished story or existing implementation does not prove the causal link. |
| V06 | Scope and method necessity | State material inclusions, exclusions, and the conditions behind them. Distinguish durable commitments from revisable methods; a particular process, tool, or sequence becomes mandatory only for a demonstrated applicable reason. |
| V07 | Conditional priorities and acceptable tradeoffs | For consequential conflicts the project is likely to face, explain what it prioritizes, what costs or losses it accepts, and under which conditions. Preserve non-exchangeable boundaries and unresolved value choices; neither a list of desirable outcomes nor invented universal weights settles a conflict. |
| V08 | Whole-result cost and sustainability | Make direction-changing resource, attention, maintenance, opportunity-cost, time-horizon, and sustainability assumptions intelligible. Explain commercial or other sustaining logic where relevant without forcing every project into a business model; separate credible repeated use from speculative future payoff. Apply the global comparison method rather than reproducing it. |
| V09 | Risk, uncertainty, and recoverability | Make project-specific material risk boundaries and assumptions available, including consequences for others and recovery limits. Derive sufficient protection from the Human-Agent Principles and the Vision's commitments, using those conditions as references that test its necessity and scope; neither zero-risk perfection nor an assumed willingness to accept harm follows from a mission. Detailed mechanisms belong downstream. |
| V10 | Decision sufficiency and authority | Confirmed commitments plus relevant facts support a bounded choice or a precise account of the missing premise. Distinguish applying an accepted tradeoff from changing one; a Vision, a qualification verdict, or a good recommendation does not authorize execution. |
| V11 | Path and dependencies | Explain how the main steps or mutually supporting directions move toward the mission and what must become true for them to work. Preserve confirmed dependencies without inventing a linear path; detailed current phases and gates belong to Roadmap. Outputs and activity alone are not progress toward value. |
| V12 | Discriminating feedback and experiments | Explain how the project obtains relevant information, detects important gaps, and uses real outcomes to support or refute empirical claims. Make load-bearing limits in observation, analysis, solution, or verification capacity intelligible, including when improving that capacity is worth the cost before choosing an experiment. Guide a finite comparison with the current approach or another relevant alternative. Benefits, costs, affected parties, qualitative judgments, quantitative observations, and uncertainty are chosen for the claim; measurement volume or modification completion is not success. Specific sources, indicators, samples, thresholds, windows, and operating steps belong to the source, experiment, or loop authority. |
| V13 | Learning and revisability | Explain how results lead to adoption, adjustment, narrowing, withdrawal, or further observation, how prior conclusions and gains inform the next iteration, and how the learning method itself is checked. Make the project's commitment to obtaining and applying reliable learning intelligible, including when worthwhile opportunities or scale justify more learning capacity and which project values bound that investment. Detailed frequency, parallelism, and resource choices belong downstream; activity quotas and shortened necessary observation do not establish faster learning. Contrary evidence or changed conditions can reopen foundations; human commitments change under P1 and empirical premises with evidence. A new stage does not itself stop an established learning loop. |
| V14 | Human readability and sufficient concision | The main text alone gives a new reader the project's identity, value, causal path, important commitments, tradeoffs, and learning logic. Use direct, connected language; remove repetition without deleting necessary reasons or boundaries. Essential premises are not hidden in a Reference, history, or agent-only vocabulary. On revision, rewrite or merge existing commitments, premises, and tradeoffs before adding new ones; each added sentence earns its place only when removing it would leave a real decision underivable or wrongly derived. Dated observations and test evidence stay out of the main text; they live in the decision history or with their evidence owner, which the main text may link where a premise needs traceable evidence. No word count or decorative format establishes quality. |
| V15 | Coherence and derivation | Mission, principles, facts, tradeoffs, and path fit together and respect the applicable global foundations. State material tensions rather than silently choosing one clause; downstream proposals trace to specific commitments and facts. A future uncertainty is not automatically a contradiction. |
| V16 | Authority, provenance, and document boundaries | One current Vision is discoverable from the project entry, its status and confirmation scope are truthful, and material changes have traceable rationale and history. Account for substantive additions, adjustments, and removals relative to the previous version. Vision and the team's shared external information-sources directory explicitly link to each other; directory membership does not establish evidence for a premise. The main Vision owns direction; a Reference expands evidence/examples and yields to it; decision history preserves context, alternatives, authorization, supersession, and review conditions. Mutable operational state, detailed procedures, task receipts, and architecture remain with their owners. |

**Judgment.** A qualified reader judges semantic sufficiency with direct access to the relevant sources. Machines can check formal structure, identifiers, paths, and source bindings, not whether a value tradeoff is justified. Use representative consequential decisions to test whether the Vision actually supports a recommendation, a rejection or scope limit, and identification of a genuinely missing premise. Select cases and independent judgment in proportion to impact under P2; reuse still-valid observations. Equally supported methods need not produce identical wording or one universal answer. For a changed reading route, observe the actual consumer's receipt, reading, and application at that decision.

Report which criteria are supported, deficient, or unknown, with scope, material reasons, and evidence; group criteria that share a rationale. A material unresolved deficiency or unknown prevents an unqualified claim of fitness for the affected decision. Qualification is not project success, proof of every hypothesis, or a numeric score. Continue independent authorized work while the affected choice remains provisional under the global derivation-gap rule. This standard is revisable when a demonstrated reusable failure exposes a missing dimension; it is not a claim that all future decisions are specified.

### Project learning documents

[[claude/rules/project-rsi]] owns the shared learning method, personal-review boundary, and loop qualification; its paired-runtime branch owns the selected independent-learning and synthesis method. A project's RSI document or inline Workflow section owns that project's operating choices and links its current Vision, information sources, authorization, and learning records. Split an RSI document only when its reader value or independent change cadence warrants it; [[templates/project-rsi-template]] is writing scaffolding, not another method authority. Research retention and its boundary with execution follow [[claude/rules/project-rsi#Learning records]] and [[claude/rules/tasks-rules]]; storing a candidate does not assign or dispatch work.

The team's shared external-source directory is a `reference`, normally `information-sources.md` at the project's existing accessible document authority. It serves human teammates and agents across project understanding, research, design, decisions, delivery, and RSI. The homepage, Vision, and RSI link the same directory; the directory explicitly links the applicable current Vision. Use vault-absolute wikilinks in the vault and document links at a repository-owned surface, preserving both directions in rendered navigation. Vision-derived candidate coverage, user selection, source definitions and uses follow [[claude/rules/project-rsi#Information sources]]; [[templates/information-sources-template]] supplies a concise starting shape. The directory helps readers locate information; observed results and retrieval receipts stay with their evidence owners.

## Agent L2 Architecture

Agent L2 Architecture is the project architecture contract. It is agent-only: the writing is optimized for agent orientation and constraint, while remaining ordinary, auditable prose. C4 contributes the useful Context and Container map ideas but is not the document identity, and Component or Code layers are not required architecture documents.

A project with active L2 content has exactly one discoverable `architecture_role: entry`. The entry uses `reader: agent` and begins with exactly named H2 sections `System scope`, `Container and domain map`, and `Reading routes` in that order; it may append a compact project-specific contract only when a current consumer needs one. These sections define the system scope, the Container/Domain map, the reading route to every current L2 domain, and the glossary route when one exists. Every current or evergreen `architecture_role: domain` is reachable from that entry by direct or transitive vault-absolute wikilinks, names the entry in `source`, and uses exactly these four H2 sections in this order:

1. `Container topology`
2. `Authority and state ownership`
3. `Trust boundaries and invariants`
4. `Durable decisions`

`Authority and state ownership` covers the semantic owner of data, rules, roles, lifecycle, evidence, and other authoritative state relevant to the domain. A glossary is optional and gets `architecture_role: glossary`; create it only for real project-specific, cross-domain, or easily confused terms, never as an empty carrier.

Admit a fact to L2 only when all are true: an agent cannot reconstruct it cheaply and reliably from live authority; it changes where the agent should look, modify, or place trust; it is stable enough to outlive ordinary implementation churn; and it has a clear semantic owner. Route the rest to its live owner:

| Fact | Owner |
| --- | --- |
| Routes, endpoints, schemas, classes, functions, algorithms | Code and executable contracts |
| User behavior and acceptance | L1 product documents |
| Commands and operating steps | Runbooks |
| Runtime versions, deployment state, temporary workarounds | Runtime or mechanism authority |
| Incidents and historical evidence | Provenance |
| Task progress and task-period judgment | TaskNote |

Machines may validate the exact audience and role markers, one entry, the ordered entry headings, the four domain headings, resolvable links/source targets, and entry-to-domain reachability. They do not infer semantic sufficiency from wording or regex. A qualified semantic reader decides whether owner/trust/decision coverage is sufficient, whether implementation HOW leaked into L2, whether two documents compete for one fact, whether current architecture matches live reality, and whether a retired concept returned under an equivalent name.

## Body and change discipline

Write current truth for the named reader. Outside the four required Agent L2 domain sections, include only sections that carry content; do not generate empty Tasks, Open Questions, Decisions, or fixed headings. Lasting rationale belongs in the producing TaskNote Decision or the current authority when that reader needs it. Historical Decisions are not rewritten to make a current migration look tidy.

When live architecture truth changes, update its entry/domain in the same candidate. Migrate consumers before retiring the old owner, then prove current consumer closure and link reachability. Preserve unrelated history and use lazy migration for documents outside the changed scope.
